items.title: Social media marketing for authors: a practical BookTok strategy
items.author: Glasshouse
items.excerpt: How authors can build a recognisable presence between book launches, with lessons from our work with Caroline Montague.
body:
An author’s social presence needs a life between publication dates. Cover reveals and launch announcements matter, but a reader who has never encountered your work needs a reason to care before being asked to buy. A useful BookTok strategy gives that reader several ways in: the stories you tell, the subjects you find fascinating and the person behind the books.

Our work with novelist Caroline Montague offers a practical starting point. We built a video-led social presence around her world, bringing her writing, reading and surroundings into the creative direction. The lesson for other authors is to identify what makes their own work interesting, then make it understandable to a stranger.
H:Build around the reader’s interests

Start by describing your reader more precisely than “someone who loves books”. Do they enjoy historical settings, complicated families, escapist locations or a particular kind of relationship? These details help you choose subjects that connect your writing with conversations readers already want to have.

Turn each subject into a repeatable series. A historical novelist might share a research discovery that changed a scene. A thriller writer could explain how they create tension without revealing a twist. A reading recommendation can introduce your taste while giving the viewer something useful immediately.

Before filming, write ten distinct ideas beneath each series. If the list runs dry after two, you probably have a single post rather than a lasting content theme.

body.caption: Caroline Montague’s social grid: recurring settings and a recognisable personal presence give readers several ways into an author’s world. View counts shown are from the original capture.
body.alt: Caroline Montague social video grid, showing recurring scenes of reading, writing and life at home

body: H:Make every video work for someone new

Open with the interesting detail. “The letter that changed how I wrote this character” gives a new viewer a clear subject. “Another writing update” asks them to bring an interest they may not yet have.

Keep the video focused on one idea and leave enough context for the viewer to follow it. Captions should explain the subject naturally. Use relevant genre and topic language where it helps describe the piece; avoid filling the caption with unrelated tags.

You can be personal without sharing everything. Decide which parts of your working life you are comfortable making public, then build within those boundaries. A sustainable strategy should fit the author as well as the audience.

body.caption: Books sit alongside places, reading and everyday life: a useful balance between introducing the author’s world and giving a specific title room to stand out.
body.alt: Caroline Montague social grid combining A Paris Secret book imagery with travel and personal scenes

body: H:Connect discovery with the next step

Plan a mix of discovery content, deeper introductions to your books and clear publication updates. Keep purchase and newsletter information easy to find. When a post introduces a particular title, check that a curious viewer can reach the right book rather than having to search through an unclear profile.

Review results by purpose. Reach tells you how far an idea travelled; profile visits and relevant questions show curiosity; tracked website visits and newsletter registrations give you a clearer view of action. A popular video is not proof of book sales.

Begin with a filming session you can repeat, review the response and develop the strongest series. You do not need to impersonate another successful author to build a distinctive presence.

Explore the Caroline Montague case study in our Work section, or contact Glasshouse about social strategy and content creation for authors.

items.title: Social media marketing for wellness brands: build trust before the sale
items.author: Glasshouse
items.excerpt: A practical content framework for fitness studios, movement apps and wellness brands, informed by Hip & Healthy and Grace & Form.
body:
Wellness content often asks people to change something: try a class, establish a routine or make room for a new product. Before someone does that, they need to understand what you offer and whether it fits their life. Social media marketing for wellness brands should help them make that decision.

Glasshouse’s work spans wellness publishing through Hip & Healthy and ballet and movement through Grace & Form. Those businesses have different offers, but both give us a useful perspective on the balance between editorial interest, a recognisable voice and a clear commercial next step.
H:Answer the questions people ask before joining

Build your first content plan from customer questions. For a movement studio, these might include what a beginner needs, how a first session works and which class fits a short lunch break. For a wellness product, they might concern how to use it, storage or what is included.

Give each question its own post. “What you need for your first online ballet class” is a clearer idea than a broad promise to transform someone’s routine. Show the setup, demonstrate the experience and explain any relevant limitations.

Keep expertise visible. Introduce the person teaching or explaining the subject and make their role clear. Review statements about results carefully; describe what the service offers without inventing outcomes or presenting one customer’s experience as a guarantee.

body.caption: Grace & Form: performance, teaching and studio moments create several routes into ballet content. This historical views snapshot illustrates content variety; views alone do not establish trial bookings or sales.
body.alt: Grace and Form historical video views grid showing ballet performance and studio content

body: H:Create an editorial rhythm people recognise

Use four practical themes: useful guidance, people behind the business, the experience itself and the offer. Guidance answers questions; people provide context; demonstrations make the service tangible; offer posts explain how to take part.

For a studio, one filming session could capture a teacher introduction, a first-class walkthrough, a short movement demonstration and answers to common booking questions. Plan separate openings for each piece so every edit has a purpose.

Hip & Healthy illustrates the breadth of an editorial approach: a wellness audience can be interested in travel, movement, everyday habits and the people shaping those subjects. Your brand should choose its own relevant territory rather than trying to cover everything.

body.caption: Hip & Healthy’s Instagram grid combines travel, food, products and everyday wellbeing. The shared visual tone makes varied editorial subjects feel part of the same publication.
body.alt: Hip and Healthy Instagram grid showing travel, food, beauty and wellbeing photography

body: H:Measure interest and action separately

Choose a commercial priority before deciding which numbers matter. A studio seeking trial bookings needs a clear route from its profile to the relevant class or membership page. A publisher might prioritise article visits or newsletter registrations instead.

Review saves and shares for useful content, profile activity for curiosity and tracked landing-page visits for the next stage. Then compare those visits with completed bookings or registrations. Avoid treating every view as a potential sale.

A manageable first month could test three recurring series, one clear offer and a weekly review of customer questions. Expand the ideas that help the right people understand the business; revise those that attract attention without relevant interest.

See our Hip & Healthy and Grace & Form projects in Work, or speak to Glasshouse about social media management for your wellness business.

items.title: Hospitality social media: turn a beautiful place into a reason to book
items.author: Glasshouse
items.excerpt: How hotels, villas and country houses can build a content plan around the stay, the guest and the questions that shape a booking.
body:
A beautiful property gives you something to photograph. A hospitality social media strategy explains why someone should spend their time there. The difference is in the detail: who the stay suits, how a day unfolds and what makes this place worth choosing.

Our hospitality work includes Villa Sartiano and Sandon Hall. A private villa and a country-house venue need different stories and different enquiry journeys. The right content plan begins with the guest and the booking decision, then works backwards to the pictures.
H:Show the experience beyond the wide shot

Keep the architectural hero images, but build a wider picture of the visit. Film arrival, the route into a room, the breakfast table, a favourite view and the spaces guests actually spend time in. Sequence those details so a viewer can imagine being there.

Write specific openings: “A slow morning at a private Tuscan villa” or “What your guests see when they arrive for a country-house wedding”. Use only descriptions that accurately fit the property and the experience available.

Our Villa Sartiano work centres on the character of the place, including its interiors, gardens and surroundings. The transferable lesson is to find your property’s own distinctive details rather than reproduce another venue’s aesthetic.

body.caption: A table set for a shared meal makes a stay tangible: it gives the viewer an occasion to imagine, alongside the architecture and setting.
body.alt: Covered stone terrace with a long dining table, blue cushions and views into the garden

body: H:Build the calendar around booking questions

Separate inspiration from practical decision-making. Inspiration earns an introduction; practical posts help someone work out whether to enquire. Create content about accommodation arrangements, event spaces, seasonal experiences and travel information that the property has checked.

Collect questions from the reservations or events team each month. Turn the recurring ones into posts, Stories and useful profile highlights. If people repeatedly ask about capacity or what is included, make that information easier to find.

Plan filming around real seasonal changes and the periods you need to support. A winter gathering requires different footage from a summer garden stay. Capture enough alternative compositions for vertical video, portrait images and website use while the space is prepared.

body.caption: Sandon Hall: an establishing image explains the scale and setting. Pair this kind of view with practical details about the stay, event or occasion people can book.
body.alt: Sandon Hall country house seen across its lawns and sweeping driveway

body: H:Make the route to an enquiry simple

Match the call to action to the content. A wedding post should lead towards wedding information; a villa-stay post should help someone check the relevant accommodation or availability. Sending everyone to an unrelated homepage adds unnecessary work.

When working with guest or creator content, agree what the property can reuse before building a campaign around it. Keep a clear record of permissions and identify the formats needed for each channel.

Measure useful interest alongside reach: relevant enquiries, visits to booking pages and the questions potential guests ask. Record where enquiries came from where possible, while recognising that people may discover a property on social and book later through another route.

Explore Villa Sartiano and Sandon Hall in our Work section, or talk to Glasshouse about hospitality content creation and social media management.

items.title: Fashion social media strategy: give people a reason to wear your brand
items.author: Glasshouse
items.excerpt: From product detail to styling and launch content: a practical framework for independent fashion brands, with a perspective from Gigi Clothing.
body:
An independent fashion brand has to communicate more than what a garment looks like. People want to understand how it moves, how they might style it and what makes it belong in their wardrobe. Your social strategy should answer those questions while giving the brand a recognisable point of view.

With Gigi Clothing, Glasshouse built the social strategy from the beginning. That experience reinforces a useful principle for emerging labels: a distinctive product gives content a strong starting point, but you still need a repeatable way to introduce it to new people.
H:Translate the product into specific content ideas

Choose three things a viewer should understand about the garment. Those could be its silhouette, construction and styling versatility. Film evidence for each: movement for the silhouette, a close-up for a construction detail and several complete outfits for styling.

A product description becomes more interesting when it answers a real question. “Three ways to style a micro mini with pieces you already own” has a clearer purpose than “Meet our latest drop”. Make sure every styling suggestion suits the actual product and your customer.

Use clean product photography alongside footage of the clothing being worn. The images serve different decisions: one clarifies the object; the other helps someone imagine it in their own life.

body.caption: Gigi Clothing: a close product view and a short, confident opening keep the garment central. The view figure belongs to this historical capture.
body.alt: Gigi Clothing short-form product post showing a silver mini skirt with an on-screen hook

body: H:Plan the launch as a sequence

Build a launch around discovery, understanding and availability. Early content can introduce a design decision or show the garment in motion. Later posts can answer practical questions about fit, colour and care before directing people to the right product page.

Avoid letting the launch consume the whole account. Develop series that remain useful between drops: styling combinations, founder decisions, customer questions and details people might miss in a single photograph.

For creator collaborations, brief the situation and the product facts, then give the creator room to speak in their own voice. Agree deliverables, review stages and reuse permissions before the content becomes essential to your calendar.

body.caption: A second Gigi example turns a product detail into a playful conversation starter. Repeating a clear format can make a series recognisable without repeating the same post. View figure shown is historical.
body.alt: Gigi Clothing post showing black mini shorts with a wide belt and a playful text hook

body: H:Learn which creative earns useful attention

Review performance at the level of the idea. Did styling content attract saves? Did a demonstration generate product questions? Did the people visiting the website explore the featured garment?

Use tracked links where practical and compare content periods with product-page visits, basket activity and sales. Stock availability, price and the shopping experience all affect conversion, so a strong video alone cannot explain the whole result.

Make the next filming session more deliberate. Keep the promising format, vary the opening or styling situation and see whether the response holds across several posts. One successful edit is a useful clue, not a complete strategy.

See the Gigi Clothing project in Work, or contact Glasshouse about social strategy, filming and ongoing social media management for fashion brands.

items.title: Podcast social media strategy: choose clips that earn the full listen
items.author: Glasshouse
items.excerpt: How to turn long conversations into clear, compelling social content without losing the context that makes the episode worth hearing.
body:
An hour-long conversation can contain dozens of possible social clips. The useful question is which moments give a new viewer a reason to listen further. A podcast social media strategy needs editorial judgement as well as editing: what is the idea, why does it matter and how much context does someone need?

Glasshouse’s podcast work includes Wolfe Power Club and Breaking the Taboo. An energy-industry conversation and a personal advocacy interview need different treatments, but both depend on making a specific moment understandable outside the full episode.
H:Select a complete idea before choosing a duration

Look for moments with a clear question, a meaningful answer and an identifiable audience. A surprising explanation, a practical observation or a personal turning point can each make a strong starting point. An isolated dramatic sentence may attract attention while misrepresenting the conversation.

Watch the proposed clip without the previous five minutes. Check whether a stranger can identify the subject, understand the speaker’s role and follow the point. Keep enough context to preserve the meaning, particularly when discussing sensitive experiences.

There is no single duration that makes every clip effective. Edit to the thought, remove repetition and review whether the opening makes the subject clear quickly enough.

body.caption: Breaking the Taboo: a specific on-screen subject gives a viewer context before they know the wider conversation. The caption should also identify the speaker and link to the relevant full episode. View figure shown is historical.
body.alt: Breaking the Taboo social clip with a speaker and an on-screen headline about maternity care

body: H:Give each episode several different entry points

Plan a small set of distinct assets instead of several near-identical extracts. One clip could introduce the central question; another could offer a useful explanation; a quote card could capture a concise observation; a later post could respond to a listener’s question.

Write titles around the actual subject. “Why this energy project takes years to build” gives a new viewer more context than “Episode 12 is live”. Keep captions readable and check names and technical terms against the recording.

Provide guests with an organised set of approved assets and the correct episode link. Agree any sensitive extracts through the appropriate review process before scheduling them.

body.caption: A second Breaking the Taboo example centres one clear statement. For sensitive conversations, keep enough context for the meaning to remain accurate and make the original source easy to find. View figure shown is historical.
body.alt: Breaking the Taboo social excerpt featuring a speaker in red and a headline about an experience of maternity care

body: H:Connect social reach with listening behaviour

Make the next step obvious. Name the podcast and episode, then direct interested viewers to the relevant listening destination. Check that the link opens the episode you are promoting.

Track clip reach and engagement separately from episode plays, follows and returning listeners. A high-view clip can be valuable discovery content without producing an equally large increase in listening. Compare release periods and referral data where available, while allowing for the limits of cross-platform attribution.

Use audience responses to improve both promotion and production. Repeated questions can suggest a follow-up extract, a clearer explanation or a future episode topic. The social plan then becomes a source of editorial insight rather than a final task after recording.

Explore Wolfe Power Club and Breaking the Taboo in Work, or speak to Glasshouse about podcast content creation and social media management.

items.title: How to choose a social media agency: what to ask before you sign
items.author: Glasshouse
items.excerpt: A clear guide to comparing social media agencies, from creative scope and filming to reporting, approvals and day-to-day ownership.
body:
Choosing a social media agency is partly a creative decision and partly an operational one. You need work that feels right for the brand, alongside a clear understanding of who will plan, produce, approve and publish it. A polished pitch cannot answer those questions on its own.

Before comparing proposals, write down the business problem you want to solve. It might be inconsistent output, a shortage of original footage, a new launch or an audience that does not yet understand the offer. That brief gives you a more useful basis for comparison than a headline number of posts.
H:Ask how the strategy becomes weekly work

Request an explanation of the proposed audience, the role of each channel and the content themes the agency would explore. Then ask how those choices become a filming brief and a calendar.

A useful answer should connect creative ideas with the business. For a hospitality brand, that might mean balancing destination appeal with booking questions. For an author, it could mean building interest between publication dates. Sector experience helps when the team can explain the decisions behind the work.

Review relevant case studies in context. Ask about the starting point, time period, scope and whether paid media contributed. Views, followers and enquiries describe different outcomes; none should be treated as interchangeable.

body.caption: Ask an agency to explain the thinking behind relevant work. Caroline Montague’s grid gives a concrete starting point: who the content is for, which themes repeat and how those choices connect with an author’s goals. Figures shown are historical.
body.alt: Caroline Montague video grid used as an example of an author marketing portfolio

body: H:Compare the actual scope

Clarify what “content creation” includes. Is the agency filming original footage, designing assets from your materials or editing existing clips? Ask how often filming happens, what preparation you provide and how additional production is agreed.

Confirm whether a quoted number of posts means original ideas or placements across channels. Four concepts adapted for two platforms is different from eight separate concepts. Neither is automatically better; the distinction helps you assess the plan fairly.

Ask about captions, scheduling, community replies, creator coordination and revisions. Agree the approval process, response times and the person responsible for each stage. A realistic workflow prevents a strong idea from becoming a last-minute request for missing assets.

body.caption: Compare the creative approach across sectors: this Gigi Clothing product post has a different job from an author’s personal content. Ask how the agency will adapt its work to your customers, rather than simply repeat a successful format. View figure shown is historical.
body.alt: Gigi Clothing mini skirt post illustrating a product-focused approach to social content

body: H:Choose reporting that supports decisions

Ask to see how the agency reviews work and what it changes as a result. Useful reporting explains which subjects and formats attracted relevant interest, where people took a next step and what the team plans to test next.

Agree a small set of measures tied to your goal, then keep reach and engagement in context. For enquiries or sales, establish what can be tracked and what attribution will remain uncertain. Be cautious of precise commercial promises that do not account for your offer, website or sales process.

Finally, confirm access arrangements, ownership of assets, handover expectations and what happens when the scope changes. The right partnership should be understandable before it starts.
